title: The Drive on Moscow
subtitle: The principal opening of Operation Typhoon.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: The main assault threatens the armies west of Moscow as Soviet telephone records reveal urgent reports, promised reinforcements and uncertain arrivals.
body:
A plan becomes a battle

On 2 October 1941, the northern and central arms of Typhoon joined Guderian's attack in the south. Hoth's Third Panzer Group and Hoepner's Fourth Panzer Group were to break through on opposite sides of the Soviet defence and converge near Vyazma. Infantry armies would widen the breaches and contain the forces caught behind the armour. The plan sought to deprive Moscow of the field armies protecting it before attempting the next advance. Its scale was immense, but the strategic question remained unresolved: would another destruction of Soviet forces finally end the state's capacity to continue fighting, or leave Germany facing another army farther east? [1][2]

The German command wanted a decisive destruction of the Soviet field armies before the capital. A city can be approached along a road, but an enemy army must be fixed, bypassed and prevented from withdrawing. That difference explains the shape of Typhoon. The northern pincer was to move from the Velizh sector, the southern part of the Vyazma pincer from the Roslavl region, and the wider right wing towards Orel. Infantry armies were essential to hold the shoulders of the breakthroughs and deal with forces left behind. German leaders expected success in this first stage to create a new strategic situation; the destruction of Soviet armies was not an incidental task on the way to the city.[2][3]

Each attacking command had to overcome a different portion of the Soviet defence before the planned convergence could occur. Success on one wing could make the other wing's task more urgent rather than complete it. Soviet commanders, meanwhile, needed to identify the decisive penetrations and determine whether reserves could stop them or whether withdrawal was necessary to preserve their forces. The opening battle was therefore a contest over reaction as much as striking power. German concentration created the opportunity for a breakthrough; exploitation required the attackers to move faster than the defenders could restore the connections between their armies and the routes behind them. [1][2][3]a

The assembled German force

Field Marshal Fedor von Bock commanded a concentration unprecedented for a single German army-group headquarters in this war. David Stahel's study places about 1.9 million men under Army Group Centre and identifies seventy-five divisions, including fourteen panzer divisions, in the enlarged force assembled for Typhoon. Its public introduction describes more than 1,500 tanks and roughly 1,000 aircraft assigned to the offensive. Such figures establish the scale of the operation, not the number of serviceable tanks that crossed each start line at dawn. They include formations with different tasks and strengths. The force was powerful precisely because it combined armour, motorised troops, infantry, artillery and air support across a very wide front.[3]

The northern arm drew on Third Panzer Group under Hermann Hoth and Ninth Army. The central and southern arm against the Vyazma position combined Fourth Panzer Group under Erich Hoepner with Fourth Army. Farther south, Guderian's Second Panzer Group and Second Army were assigned the Bryansk–Orel problem. These formations did not carry identical loads or attack identical terrain. The armoured groups aimed for operational depth; the armies of marching infantry had to maintain the battle's breadth and deal with surviving Soviet positions. A successful panzer thrust therefore created more work for the troops following it. The German design required these parts to move in relation to one another even as terrain and resistance made their rates of advance unequal.[1][2]

The preparation itself exposed a weakness. Fourth Panzer Group's projected force around Roslavl included divisions sent from reserve and other army groups; Third Panzer Group near Velizh also received units transferred from the north. The German planning study lists the 10th Panzer Division already near Roslavl and identifies the 2nd, 5th, 11th, 19th and 20th as part of that southern Vyazma concentration. It places the 7th, 1st and 6th in the projected northern force. These lists describe planned assignments, not identical fighting strength or proof that every division moved on 2 October. Some units had travelled hundreds of miles across the front simply to be ready. Their movement consumed fuel and vehicle life before the offensive began.[2][1][3]b

The three mobile thrusts

The northern and central panzer groups approached Vyazma from opposite sides, while Guderian’s Second Panzer Group threatened Bryansk Front farther south. Each thrust had a separate task. Infantry support and communications had to connect them before their advances could produce the intended enclosures.[2]c

The Soviet line is not one line

Opposite Bock stood a Soviet system of three fronts rather than an undifferentiated mass. Ivan Konev commanded the Western Front; Semyon Budenny held the Reserve Front; Andrei Eremenko commanded the Bryansk Front in the south. The U.S. Army history gives their combined strength at no less than 1.25 million. That number shows a substantial rebuilding effort after the summer's losses. It should not be read as 1.25 million soldiers equally available to meet one German breach. Fronts covered different sectors, and their armies were separated by distances, transport requirements and command boundaries. The German plan deliberately sought to exploit those divisions in the Soviet position.[1]

The Soviet deployment offered depth, but depth could become isolation if the connections between its positions were cut. Western Front held the forward approaches; Reserve Front's armies occupied positions behind and among them, while Bryansk Front faced the southern threat. The German thrusts were intended to pass around these forces and sever their routes east. An army could therefore suffer a strategic defeat before all its divisions had been driven from their trenches. The danger was that formations still facing the original attack would discover that the roads to their headquarters, supplies and neighbouring armies had been occupied behind them. Typhoon aimed to make local resistance increasingly difficult to coordinate. [1]

The September defence plan relied partly on reserves moving between sectors, including by rail. That required warning and usable routes. Several simultaneous penetrations could create competing demands before a reserve completed its first journey. The disaster that followed therefore cannot be explained as the absence of any Soviet provision for depth or flank protection. German attacks could destroy the communications and movement on which those provisions depended.[5][1]d

The numerical rebuilding of the Red Army had not removed differences in training, equipment or experience between formations. Some units had survived the summer battles at heavy cost; others were recent creations. The German concentration was designed to bring powerful mobile forces against selected sectors of this uneven defence. It did not require superiority at every point. Once a penetration succeeded, units on a neighbouring stretch of front could lose their position through a threat to their flank even if they had held against the enemy directly before them. That interaction helps explain why the size of the Soviet force did not by itself prevent a rapidly developing catastrophe. [1]

An early-morning telephone exchange on 2 October gives a closer view of Bryansk Front’s uncertainty. Chief of staff Georgy Zakharov reported Sevsk lost and German tanks moving towards Dmitrovsk-Orlovsky; Eremenko was away with the troops. The command was committing the 42nd Tank Brigade, moving the 287th Rifle Division by rail and coordinating protection of the Oka crossings with the Orel Military District. Stalin promised two rifle divisions and two tank brigades through Orel on 3–4 October. These were commitments made during a crisis, not verified arrivals at the front.[6][1]e

The attack from two directions

The northern and central attacks on 2 October unfolded on approaches with different relationships to Vyazma. Hoth's Third Panzer Group moved from the Velizh region towards the northern side of the intended enclosure. Hoepner's Fourth Panzer Group struck from the Roslavl sector towards the southern side. Ninth and Fourth Armies supported the larger design with infantry and artillery. The advancing groups were not heading straight east in parallel; each had to turn into a position from which it could close behind Soviet armies. A report of forward progress from one wing therefore did not prove that the other had kept pace. The pincer metaphor is useful only while we remember that each arm consisted of men, vehicles and headquarters fighting on separate roads.[2][1]

Guderian's thrust through the Orel direction extended the threat well south of Vyazma. The German plan sent his force from the Glukhov region towards Orel, with further movement towards Moscow dependent on the opening operation's success. Bryansk Front therefore had to confront a blow reaching around its southern side while German Second Army pressed from the west. The defenders could not treat Guderian's movement as a distant raid: it threatened the connections needed to supply their forces and withdraw them east. For the Germans, however, the wider sweep also increased the ground their infantry and transport would have to cover behind the armour. [2][1]f

The southern breakthrough also drew a large air commitment on paper. Stavka directive 002507 assigned four long-range air divisions and the 81st Special-Purpose Air Division against German forces around Glukhov and Sevsk, under General Rukhle, with fighter cover from Bryansk Front. The order establishes the priority given to this sector. It does not count serviceable aircraft, completed sorties or their results: air support, like ground reinforcement, still had to reach a changing battlefield.[6]

Artillery and infantry preparation mattered even when armoured movement attracted the headlines. Tanks seeking an opening needed enemy strongpoints suppressed or bypassed, engineers to deal with obstacles and bridges, and roads kept sufficiently clear for the columns behind them. Infantry armies could pin defenders in place while mobile formations searched for depth; they could also be left with the harder work of fighting encircled troops after the vehicles had driven on. In that relationship lay both the power and the vulnerability of Typhoon. If the mobile units moved too slowly, defenders might escape the intended enclosure. If they moved too quickly without support, the route back to fuel and ammunition could remain insecure. A first-day report of miles gained could not settle which risk was emerging.[2][1][3][6]g

Expectation and doubt

The command records show confidence surviving beside evidence of danger. In the early hours of 1 October, Eremenko described the previous day’s breakthrough and proposed a counterattack using troops in his sector and the incoming 42nd Tank Brigade. He presented the penetration as something that could still be contained and attacked on its flanks. This was his assessment to Stalin as events unfolded, rather than a reconstruction informed by the eventual defeat.[6]

Eremenko’s conversation also exposed the limits on that proposed response. Rain and snow were hindering flying and wheeled traffic, he reported, while rocket ammunition was running down. He asked for replenishment through Orel, and Stalin offered more aircraft. Operational confidence and material difficulty appeared in the same exchange. Having a counterattack in mind did not mean possessing all the means to carry it out.[6]

By 2 October, Zakharov was reporting further German movement and another set of commitments and requests. Read together, the conversations show an assessment being overtaken by events. Headquarters had to make decisions while reports, enemy formations and reinforcements travelled at different speeds. Fresh orders could express determination without restoring the conditions needed for a coherent front.[6]h

On the Soviet side, a defensive system that preserved its men and weapons could still fail if headquarters lost the ability to move them where they were needed. Holding every position was not necessarily compatible with preserving an army: an exposed formation might need to retreat before the enemy closed its route. Yet withdrawal also surrendered ground protecting Moscow and risked disrupting neighbouring units. The opening attack forced commanders to make those choices before the full pattern of the German advance was clear. The later disaster emerged through these operational problems, not from a predetermined absence of Soviet strength or willingness to resist. [1]i

For Eremenko and Zakharov, the immediate problem was keeping their forces functioning through the next German advance. Aircraft promised by higher command and ammunition requested from a depot belonged to that urgent struggle. The records establish what was requested and instructed. Whether the resources reached the troops soon enough was a further question that those conversations could not settle.[6]j

The economy beyond the battlefield

The limits of a quick decision extended beyond the opposing armies. Germany had occupied important Soviet territory since June, but the military economy continued to operate across a much larger space. Conquest could remove mines, factories and railways from Soviet use without transferring their output intact to the occupier; evacuation and demolition further complicated the calculation. The economic value of the next advance therefore depended on what resources it denied the Soviet Union and what remained available farther east. Capturing a political centre and disabling the means of continued warfare were related objectives, but they were not interchangeable. [2]

On the very day the main offensive opened, General Georg Thomas submitted an economic assessment that challenged its promise of finality. Thomas headed the armed forces' economic and armaments organisation. His survey considered successive hypothetical German advances, asking how much productive capacity the Soviet Union would retain after each. The analysis did not assume that taking Moscow would automatically end the war. Even extensive losses of industrial territory could leave the Soviet state able to make urgently needed equipment and continue resistance. This was an internal German calculation, not Soviet propaganda. It reveals that the leadership had access to arguments against equating another successful military operation with the destruction of the enemy's capacity to fight.[2]

Thomas's scenarios moved outward from a line embracing Moscow, Leningrad, Tula and Kharkov to additional losses in the Donets Basin and at the Maikop oil fields. A further case included Gorky, with its importance to vehicle and aircraft manufacture. The final scenario considered the loss of territory west of the Volga. These were analytical cases rather than positions held or an approved timetable of conquest. In the most extensive case, Thomas still did not regard economic collapse as certain without the loss of the Urals. The argument was consequential because Bock's offensive operated within a much narrower physical horizon. Winning west of Moscow might damage the Soviet economy severely without reaching the industrial resources that could sustain another round of armies.[2]

Thomas's report supplied no guarantee that the Soviet economy would withstand every loss. Its significance was narrower and more damaging to German assumptions: the territorial gains already achieved had not decisively disabled Soviet war production, and even further conquests might fail to do so. The report gave the leadership reasons to prepare for continuing resistance. It also exposed the distance between military means and economic ambition. Bock's immediate forces could attempt to encircle armies west of Moscow; they could not carry out, in the same movement, the vastly larger occupation implied by the most far-reaching scenarios. An offensive intended to shorten the war risked opening another set of objectives. [2]k

The promise of a decisive battle

The telephone records of 1–2 October preserve a changing picture: confident assessments, requests for help and reports of further German movement. A counterattack order shows the command’s intended response. A later report may show how quickly the situation that prompted it had already changed.[6]l

One of Thomas's cases estimated that losing the cities and territory along a line including Leningrad, Moscow, Tula and Kharkov would deprive the Soviet Union of about two-thirds of its steel and aluminium production facilities. Even under that assumption, he envisaged continued manufacture of urgently needed equipment and resistance in the spring. The estimate was not a prediction that Soviet production would be unaffected. It described severe damage that might still fall short of the collapse Germany required. That distinction helps explain the report's strategic force: the enemy could become much weaker without becoming incapable of continuing the war. [2]m

Allied promises and battlefield time

The international dimension had advanced since the negotiations described on 30 September. Harriman reported from Moscow on 1 October that the British and American missions had reached an understanding with Stalin about supplies. His telegram said material within the agreed lists would be made available and that transportation had been discussed without a firm American commitment. He described an enthusiastic close to the conference. That was a diplomatic achievement at the moment Typhoon opened, but an understanding at a conference was not a shipment at the front. The armies west of Moscow still had to confront the immediate German concentration with the weapons they possessed or could move from Soviet stocks.[4]

Harriman also reported a separate, long list of raw materials that the missions had agreed to consider sympathetically. He regarded most of the requested types and quantities as reasonable and would recommend their addition. This was a further stage of negotiation, distinct from the supplies already authorised for the missions to offer. The distinction reveals a coalition still constructing its obligations: Soviet requests could lead to a recommendation without immediately becoming an approved allocation. Raw materials also served a different purpose from completed weapons. They could sustain manufacture, provided that factories, labour and power remained available to use them. Assistance therefore had to be fitted to a Soviet economy being reorganised under attack. [4]

The closing atmosphere also differed from the strain of the earlier meetings. Harriman described enthusiasm and Stalin's thanks to Roosevelt. That report is evidence of a successful negotiation as the American participant understood it, not of trust without limits between the governments. It nevertheless records a change from discussing requests to agreeing on material assistance. The political achievement matters because Germany's strategy depended on isolating and defeating the Soviet state before its remaining resources and international connections could sustain a prolonged war. On the day the main assault opened, the invasion faced an enemy actively arranging to continue fighting beyond the next defeat. [4]n

The first day and its unfinished work

By the end of 2 October, Army Group Centre had committed its main force. The attackers had the initiative, the advantage of a prepared concentration and a plan aimed at the links between Soviet fronts. The defenders retained substantial forces and the possibility of organised reaction, but the speed and direction of the attack threatened to prevent them from using those forces as a coherent whole. This is the moment at which numbers become less explanatory than movement. Two large armies could appear roughly comparable in aggregate while one was using mobile formations to cut behind the other's sector headquarters and the other was still trying to identify which reports described the decisive danger.[1]

The attack had opened the way to a major operational victory, but its strategic promise remained unproved. German leaders had concentrated armour and aircraft to break through selected sectors and turn behind Soviet armies. Their opponents had to restore communication and control quickly enough to keep those armies from being isolated. The fighting would decide that immediate contest. It would not, by itself, settle the questions raised in Thomas's economic survey or undo the commitments made at the Moscow conference. The German plan could succeed on the battlefield while leaving Germany engaged in a war for which that success was insufficient. [3][1]

During the next five days the German mobile groups would reach the positions from which they could close the Vyazma enclosure and cut across Bryansk Front. The forces caught behind them would remain armed, organised to varying degrees and capable of resistance. The offensive's next task would therefore differ from its first: maintaining the enclosures while preparing to move on Moscow. On 2 October that work still lay ahead. Bock had committed the main strength of Army Group Centre to the promised decisive battle, and the Soviet command was confronting an attack aimed at the connections on which its entire western defence depended. [1][3]o
